study_identification.title: Nomograms of human hippocampal volume shifted by polygenic scores

study_characteristics.study_objective: To examine the impact of genetic adjustment (using hippocampal volume polygenic scores) on hippocampal volume nomograms and their translational ability to detect dementia patients, demonstrating whether genetic information can improve the clinical utility of population norms derived from brain imaging data.

hc_age.answer: mean NR; sd NR; min 44; max 82

preprocessing_pipeline.answer: FreeSurfer; NeuroCombat for harmonization with ADNI

quality_checking_detail.answer: HV outliers were excluded using mean absolute deviation with a threshold of 5.0

site_effect_handling_detail.answer: NeuroCombat was used to adjust across ADNI sites and harmonize the volumes with the UKB dataset. 58 batches were modeled (UKB data as one batch and 57 ADNI sites as separate batches) and added ICV, sex, and diagnosis to retain biological variation.

predictor_effects.answer: Age is modeled as a fixed effect in the GPR model with a squared exponential covariance kernel function

nm_vldtn_handle_ns.reason: The study addresses some nuisance structure: (1) ICV and scan date were linearly regressed out of HV; (2) Site effects were handled using NeuroCombat harmonization between UKB and ADNI; (3) Sex stratification was performed. However, the paper does not provide comprehensive validation of the model's ability to handle all types of nuisance structure (e.g., heteroscedasticity across age, systematic variance patterns). The GPR model naturally provides variance estimates, but there is limited explicit discussion of whether these variance patterns are validated against expected distributions.
nm_vldtn_handle_ns.supporting_text: ICV and scan date were linearly regressed out of the HVs... We used NeuroCombat to adjust across ADNI sites and harmonize the volumes with the UKB dataset. To do this we modelled 58 batches (UKB data as one batch and 57 ADNI sites as separate batches) and added ICV, sex, and diagnosis... The dataset was then stratified by self-reported sex. HV outliers were excluded using mean absolute deviation with a threshold of 5.0.

nm_vldtn_same_domain_nonindep.reason: The study compares GPR-based nomograms with the sliding window approach (SWA) using the same UKB dataset, which provides some internal validation. Additionally, the study examines performance across different sample sizes (Figure 2-figure supplement 3), showing that GPR nomograms achieve similar accuracy with only 5% (900 samples) of the dataset compared to the full training set. However, explicit metrics for model validation on held-out data from the same domain (e.g., cross-validation within UKB) are not clearly reported.
nm_vldtn_same_domain_nonindep.supporting_text: Nomograms of healthy subjects generated using the sliding window approach (SWA) and GPR method displayed similar trends... Furthermore, our GPR nomograms confirmed previously reported trends... GPR nomograms achieved the same level of accuracy with only 5% (900 samples) of the dataset.

nm_vldtn_same_domain_indep.reason: The study does not appear to use an independent hold-out dataset from the same domain (UK Biobank) for validation. The UKB data (35,686 subjects) were used to train the normative models, and the ADNI dataset was used for external validation in a different domain (clinical application). There is no mention of splitting the UKB data into training and independent test sets, or using other UK Biobank participants not included in the training set for validation.
nm_vldtn_same_domain_indep.supporting_text: Using imaging data from 35,686 healthy subjects aged 44-82 from the UK Biobank (UKB), we built HV nomograms using Gaussian process regression (GPR)... Clinical impact of genetically adjusted nomograms was investigated by comparing 818 subjects from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) database... The UKB dataset was used to train the models and the ADNI dataset was used to test them.
nm_vldtn_same_domain_indep.location: Abstract and page 11, Materials and methods

nm_vldtn_diff_domain.reason: The study explicitly validates the normative models using an independent dataset from a different domain (ADNI). The ADNI dataset (n=818 after exclusions) includes cognitively normal (CN), mild cognitive impairment (MCI), and Alzheimer's disease (AD) participants aged 55-95. This represents a different population (clinical vs. healthy), different age range, different acquisition sites (57 ADNI sites vs. single UKB site), and different scanner protocols. The study applies NeuroCombat harmonization to address cross-domain differences and evaluates the nomograms' ability to detect clinical groups.
nm_vldtn_diff_domain.supporting_text: Clinical impact of genetically adjusted nomograms was investigated by comparing 818 subjects from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) database diagnosed as either cognitively normal (CN), having mild cognitive impairment (MCI) or Alzheimer's disease (AD) patients... For an application dataset, we used the ADNI database... A total of 1001 ADNI subjects (445 male) aged 55-95 were included in this analysis... We used NeuroCombat to adjust across ADNI sites and harmonize the volumes with the UKB dataset.
nm_vldtn_diff_domain.location: Abstract and page 10, Materials and methods

clinical_application_and_analysis.association_analysis: Comparison of median percentiles and standard deviations across diagnostic groups (CN, MCI, AD); ANOVA tests to evaluate genetic adjustment impact on percentile distributions; Cox proportional hazards models for MCI-to-AD conversion analysis accounting for sex and age
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_findings_brief: Genetic adjustment using HV-PGS shifted nomograms by ~100 mm³ (equivalent to 3 years of normal aging at age 65) and reduced intra-diagnostic-group variance by an average of 68% in cognitively normal subjects, though it did not improve MCI-to-AD conversion prediction.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_findings_detailed: Using HV polygenic scores (HV-PGS), genetically adjusted nomograms from participants stratified into the top and bottom 30% of HV-PGS shifted the nomograms by ~100 mm³ (2.3% of average HV), which equates to 3 years of normal aging for a person aged ~65. In the ADNI dataset, cognitively normal (CN) participants (n=225) had median bilateral HV percentile of 61% (±25% SD), MCI participants (n=391) had 25% (±26% SD), and AD participants (n=121) had 1% (±9% SD). Genetic adjustment reduced the percentile gap between high and low PGS groups: in CN samples from 10% to 1% (90% relative reduction), in MCI from 10% to 4% (60% relative reduction), and in AD from 0.9% to 0.4% (56% relative reduction), representing an average of 68% relative decrease in intra-diagnostic-group variance. However, Cox proportional hazards models showed no significant improvement in distinguishing stable (n=299) from MCI-to-AD progressing subjects (n=83), with both adjusted and non-adjusted models resulting in hazard ratio of 0.97 (p<4.87E-08). The PGS explained up to 28% of variance in bilateral HV (R²=0.28 at p-value threshold 0.75 in combined sex model). GPR nomograms extended the application age range by 20 years compared to sliding window approach (45-82 vs 52-72 years), enabling evaluation of 86% vs 56% of ADNI diagnostic groups.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_limitations: 1) PGS stratification approach requires separate nomograms rather than integrating PGS directly into GP models; 2) PGS based on GWAS of average bilateral HV may lack specificity for sex- and hemisphere-specific models; 3) Reliability concerns with FreeSurfer HV estimates which consistently overestimate HV compared to manual segmentation; 4) Large variance in PGS estimates may undermine PGS-based stratification; 5) Potential remaining site effects despite NeuroCombat harmonization; 6) The observed peak in male nomogram at 50 years may be due to edge effects from under-sampling in younger participants; 7) Limited clinical utility demonstrated - genetic adjustment did not improve MCI-to-AD conversion prediction.
clinical_application_and_analysis.application_notes: The genetic adjustment reduced phenotypic heterogeneity within diagnostic groups but did not improve prognostic accuracy for MCI-to-AD conversion, likely because pathological effects of AD on HV (~804 mm³ or 6.4% volume loss) far exceed the genetic adjustment shift (~100 mm³ or 0.8% of mean HV). Authors suggest the added precision may prove more useful in early detection of deviation among CN subjects, for instance in detecting subtle HV loss in individuals with presymptomatic neurodegeneration. The study demonstrates that accounting for polygenic effects in normative modeling is important for untangling phenotypic heterogeneity, with implications for stratifying subgroups and potentially improving sensitivity to detect early disease processes when extended to multiple brain regions.

general_notes.general_notes: This study is unique in incorporating polygenic scores for healthy variation (HV-PGS) rather than disease-associated variants (like APOE) into normative modeling. The authors note that APOE genotype stratification would chart different HV trajectories among APOE genotypes but would mask pathological decline, theoretically decreasing sensitivity to HV decline. In contrast, HV-PGS based on genetic variants influencing HV in healthy subjects (excluding dementia patients) should theoretically enable earlier detection of AD-related decline. The study compared GPR with a previously reported sliding window method (SWM) from Nobis et al., 2019, showing GPR is more data efficient and extends age range. Training GPR model with 16,000 samples took ~1 hour on consumer grade machine (2.3 GHz 8-Core Intel Core i9). The study also tested ICV-PGS and AD-PGS as controls, finding these did not result in meaningfully different nomograms compared to non-adjusted nomograms, supporting the specificity of HV-PGS effects. Exclusion criteria for UKB: 453 subjects for various conditions, 3497 for genetic ancestry (non-British), 28 outliers. For ADNI: 26 subjects for genetic ancestry (non-white non-Hispanic), 314 based on HV quality scores. Full ADNI dataset before exclusions: 1001 subjects (445 male) aged 55-95.
